title: database comparisons SQL Server PostgreSQL MySQL document stores and tradeoffs
concepts: A database comparison begins with workload and operating constraints, not a universal ranking. Model shape, transaction boundaries, query patterns, consistency needs, operational skills, availability targets, and managed-service constraints determine fit.

Relational databases represent data through tables and declared relationships, with SQL queries and transaction guarantees; SQL Server, PostgreSQL, and MySQL share concepts but differ in syntax, extensions, tooling, and behavior.

Document databases store nested records and are useful when aggregate boundaries and access patterns align with document shape. Flexible representation does not remove the need for schema evolution, indexes, validation, or consistency decisions.

Compare database engines and hosted services separately. A managed service changes operational responsibility, supported features, extensions, upgrade control, and portability even when the underlying engine has a familiar name.

Benchmarks are workload-specific. Compare realistic data size, query mix, indexes, concurrency, durability settings, hardware, cache state, and tail latency; do not treat vendor benchmark claims as general rankings.

items: SQL Server 2025 adds vector data types and functions, preview vector indexes, optimized locking, and other engine updates; keep preview status separate from generally available features.
PostgreSQL 18 is the current stable major release; PostgreSQL 19 is a release candidate at this check, not stable.
MySQL uses separate LTS and Innovation release lines; MySQL 26.10 is Innovation while 9.7 is LTS, so do not compare version numbers as one sequential stable line.
MongoDB 9.0 is the current major stable release; 8.3 is a minor release line with deployment-specific availability and should not be called the newest major.

scopeExclusions: SQL syntax and SQL Server-specific feature details are taught in t03-003 through t03-011.
Detailed MongoDB administration, Atlas configuration, and provider-specific API surfaces are outside this comparison topic.
Cloud service price lists and benchmark leaderboards are excluded because they change frequently and depend on region, edition, configuration, and workload.
Database engines and managed hosting products are distinguished; Azure SQL Database, RDS, Atlas, and DocumentDB are not interchangeable with their underlying open-source or licensed engine.
